doc.title: Howard Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: John Lennon horn sessions
summary: His story of Lennon's horn section stalling until he suggested the arrangement, then arranging the rest; Lennon's secrecy and fans.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I jotted down a few — I think it’s really fascinating that you played on “Escalator Over the Hill,” and then you played with John Lennon. Is that true?
Yes. Not at the same time.
Do you remember much about the John Lennon sessions?

Oh I’d say everything. It was a horn section. John had the track all ready and we were going to put horns on it. And he had this idea that he explained to us that horn players are real musicians, not like guys who just play guitar and drums and that sort of thing. And if you put a bunch of them together they’ll just make magic happen. Well I knew most of the other guys. I knew that wasn’t going to happen with this bunch because they were crabby and critical and stuff like that. And we spent, it was supposed to be two three hour sessions. Double session. And after that period of time we had nothing you know? I didn’t want to say anything because I’ve been in situations before with one of those characters who when I was trying to help and improve something on some other gig, he said, “Well who made you the arranger?” You know? So I’m just trying to help you know. But I didn’t say anything more after that. So we had only worked on one tune and we didn’t have anything. And I spoke up and said, “Well look at this point I know the track very well from listening to it for over two hours, and I have some ideas if nobody minds.” You know, aimed at these crabby guys. And they said, “For God’s sake yes.” So we played my ideas and that became the arrangement for that tune. And he said, he was very happy, he said, “We can do this again. Come tomorrow at the same time and we’ll work through you if you don’t mind.” I said, “No, only too glad.”
Did you get to hear the next day’s tune before you left?

No. Well not until the last day. Because it’s a very paranoid world you know. And there was stuff going on that they were trying to keep undercover. For instance, that’s when Yoko was away in China somewhere and he was with — I don’t remember that name now — May Pang. And there would always be people outside the studio, Beatle fans who wanted to give him a beaded collar or some kind of thing or something, or a poem that they wrote in 1966 in honor of him. And you never knew who was going to be there. But he finally trusted me enough to give me a cassette of the next tunes. I wrote them out at home.
Well that’s really a great story and the fact that you had that skill and could finally speak up and say I know how to make this happen. Were those other horn players, were they older than you?
I just wondered, maybe they had an attitude about.
